extracted.intended_audience: academics (especially early- and mid-career researchers) who write grant proposals and face rejection
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical/emotional strategies for researchers dealing with grant proposal rejection: how to process feedback, reuse work, maintain productivity and resilience, and improve future proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digest and address reviewer feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Take reviewers' comments seriously: spend time to understand them and respond point-by-point to improve future submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post advises that reviewers are 'unlikely to be stupid' and 'probably don’t have axes to grind.' You should 'take the time to digest what they are saying and address each of the points in turn.' Treat reviewer advice as generous input that can make your work better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat rejection as a learning opportunity (savor mistakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use rejection to learn about what went wrong and to extract improvements for future work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted advice: 'Try to acquire the weird practice of savoring your mistakes, delighting in uncovering the strange quirks that led you astray. Then, once you have sucked all the goodness to be gained from having made them, you can cheerfully set them behind you and go on to the next big opportunity' (Dennett). The emphasis is on extracting lessons before moving on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move on quickly and recycle writing
rubrics_metrics.description: After extracting lessons from the rejection, move on promptly and reuse parts of the proposal in other papers or applications where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bracing thought: 'Move on. You’re not going to remember about this for very long.' The post advises asking if what you wrote 'can be recycled for another paper, or another grant application' and if so, discard the grieving and get back to writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase proposal volume (write more to get more successes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat success as partly probabilistic: submit more proposals to raise the chance of funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author relays a manager's maxim: 'if you’re not getting rejected, you’re not writing enough proposals.' 'The more you write, the higher the likelihood of success.' This advocates productivity and throughput as a strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain optimism / a delusional sense of significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate optimism about the importance of your work as a psychological strategy to persist through repeated small failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Kahneman: 'scientific research is another domain where a form of optimism is essential to success: I have yet to meet a successful scientist who lacks the ability to exaggerate the importance of what he or she is doing.' The post frames this 'delusional' optimism as necessary to cope with the typical pattern of failures and rare successes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow emotional processing but build resilience
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge and permit the normal emotional response to rejection (grief, tears), but recognize it gets easier with experience and aim to recover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes personal experience: 'I have shed tears over various proposals and papers over the years but it does get easier.' She describes developing an attitude over about a decade that lets one 'shrug and then forget it.' The framing includes both comforting and bracing thoughts depending on where you are in the grief cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rejection to become more empathetic as a teacher/mentor
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the pain of rejection inform kinder, more constructive interaction with students and colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comforting thought #2: 'The pain you experience now will make you a better teacher.' The post suggests you will avoid harsh marking because you'll remember how rejection feels and choose to be constructive and kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek peer support and share experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Share stories of rejection with peers to receive comfort and realize the experience is common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author invites readers: 'Feeling rejected? Share your story below, and readers will comfort you. We’ve all been there!' Social sharing is presented as a source of consolation and normalization.
